summary: In dense topologies, link-state flooding can slow down convergence. This experimental document discusses the problem and an architectural solution that shrinks the flooding topology, and specifies protocol changes for IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

eli5.summary: When news spreads through a crowded room, everyone repeating it to everyone makes noise. This picks a few paths for the news to travel so it still reaches everybody with less shouting.

questions: dynamic flooding in is-is and ospf
how to reduce link-state flooding in dense networks
how does dynamic flooding improve convergence
subtitle: Optimize link-state flooding in dense network topologies to improve convergence time.

tldr.problem: In dense network topologies such as leaf-spine data centers, standard link-state flooding redundantly sends updates through many paths, causing control plane overload and delayed convergence when topology changes occur.
tldr.mechanism: Dynamic Flooding decouples the flooding topology from the physical topology by computing a reduced flooding topology that still connects all nodes but uses far fewer links, either centrally on an elected Area Leader or in a distributed manner on all participating nodes.
tldr.outcome: Networks using dynamic flooding achieve significant improvements in convergence time and control plane stability, particularly in dense topologies, while remaining compatible with non-dynamic-flooding nodes.

today: RFC 9667 is an Experimental specification published in October 2024. It provides mechanisms for IS-IS, OSPFv2, and OSPFv3 to improve performance in dense network topologies through optimized flooding.

sections.title: The Problem with Dense Topologies
sections.content:
Modern networks increasingly use dense topologies such as leaf-spine Clos fabrics in data centers and spine-leaf architectures in wide-area networks. In these topologies, a router may have many physical neighbors, creating a highly connected graph. However, standard link-state routing protocols like IS-IS and OSPF rely on a flooding algorithm that is inefficient in dense topologies.

When a router updates its link-state database and floods the update to its neighbors, each neighbor forwards it to all of its other neighbors. In a dense topology, this causes the same update to reach each node many times through different paths. While the protocol correctly handles duplicate updates by discarding them, the redundant copies consume valuable control plane bandwidth and CPU resources. When many updates arrive in rapid succession (as they do during topology changes), the control plane queue fills up, causing updates to be dropped and delaying network convergence.

The problem is not new: networks have used mechanisms like IS-IS mesh groups to reduce flooding, but these require careful manual configuration. RFC 9667 provides an automated solution: Dynamic Flooding computes a reduced flooding topology automatically.
sections.eli5: When routers share link-state information, they send it along every path. This means the same message gets repeated many times. In crowded networks, this slows everything down.

sections.title: Solution Approach and Requirements
sections.content:
Dynamic Flooding addresses the problem by decoupling the flooding topology (the set of links used to propagate updates) from the physical topology (the actual network). The flooding topology is computed such that it connects all nodes in the IGP area but uses significantly fewer links, thereby reducing redundant flooding.

A single node in the area is elected as the Area Leader, similar to how IS-IS elects a Designated Intermediate System (DIS) on a LAN. The Area Leader can operate in one of two modes:

Centralized mode: The Area Leader computes the flooding topology and distributes it through the link-state database. Nodes receive the computed topology and use only the specified links for flooding.

Distributed mode: The Area Leader advertises an algorithm identifier, and all participating nodes independently compute the same flooding topology using that algorithm.

The solution must provide dynamic routing (reachability after any topology change), improve convergence significantly, work on various dense topology types, have no single point of failure, distribute flooding load evenly, and operate smoothly in mixed networks where some routers support dynamic flooding and others do not.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending messages along all paths, the network picks a smaller set of paths that still reach everyone. One router is in charge of deciding which paths to use.

sections.title: Computing the Flooding Topology
sections.content:
The flooding topology is computed before topology changes occur, so the computation time does not contribute to convergence delay. The topology must be connected and include all nodes, ensuring that no node becomes isolated.

For resilience, the flooding topology should contain at least a cycle covering all nodes (which guarantees no single link failure causes partition) and possibly additional links to reduce the flooding diameter and improve convergence time. The exact algorithm need not be standardized for centralized mode since it is not an interoperability issue, only the encoding of the result matters.

For complete bipartite graphs (like leaf-spine topologies), RFC 9667 describes several practical topologies. A minimal flooding topology ensures every node has at least degree two (no single failure isolates it) and can be computed in linear time. A Xia topology connects all spines through a cycle and distributes remaining leaves evenly, trading lower redundancy for slightly delayed convergence in some failures. Additional links can be added to reduce diameter at the cost of increased flooding.

If parallel links exist between two nodes, an update is flooded over only one of them. Multi-access LANs can be included in the flooding topology; when a LAN is included, all edges from the LAN are treated as part of the topology.
sections.eli5: The network picks the minimum set of connections that keeps everyone connected, maybe with a few extras to make updates spread faster.

sections.title: Protocol Mechanisms and Encoding
sections.content:
Dynamic Flooding is implemented through extensions to both IS-IS and OSPF. In IS-IS, new sub-TLVs are added to the Router Capability TLV to advertise Area Leader preference and priority, the algorithms a node supports, and the flooding topology itself.

The IS-IS Area Leader Sub-TLV allows a node to indicate its eligibility and priority for becoming Area Leader, and which computation mode (centralized or distributed) and algorithm (by numeric ID) it prefers. The node with the highest priority becomes Area Leader; ties are broken by highest system ID.

The IS-ISIS Area Node IDs TLV (centralized mode only) lists the node identifiers (System ID plus pseudonode ID for LANs) in the area, with each assigned an index for compact encoding. The Flooding Path TLV encodes the flooding topology as a series of intersecting paths, where each path is a sequence of connected links. This compact representation avoids rigid encoding schemes.

OSPF uses similar mechanisms via opaque LSAs (for OSPFv2) and typed LSAs (for OSPFv3), with equivalent TLV structures. Nodes also advertise which local edges are enabled for flooding (LEEF), aiding in troubleshooting.

Transient conditions during topology changes are handled gracefully: nodes may flood on multiple flooding topologies during transients, and flooding loops during transients are handled by the standard duplicate detection mechanism.
sections.eli5: Routers exchange messages saying 'I want to lead' or 'I support this algorithm', then they all compute or receive the same set of paths to use for flooding.

sections.title: Flooding Behavior and Topology Changes
sections.content:
Under normal operation, a node only floods link-state updates on edges that are part of the calculated flooding topology. On links outside the flooding topology, database synchronization occurs via standard mechanisms (CSNP in IS-IS, database exchange in OSPF), but flooding does not occur.

When a node receives link-state information from outside the flooding topology, it indicates the sender may not have flooding topology information or has stale information. In such cases, the update is flooded on the flooding topology as well as sent normally.

If dynamic flooding has no topology information (during initial deployment or after Area Leader loss), nodes fall back to standard flooding until the flooding topology is computed and distributed.

Topology events are handled systematically: when a link not on the flooding topology fails, no action is required. When a link on the flooding topology fails, temporarily affected nodes flood on any available path until convergence. When a node is added or fails, the Area Leader recomputes the flooding topology and distributes it. When the Area Leader itself fails, a new Area Leader is elected and computes a new flooding topology, overwriting the old one.

Recovery from multiple simultaneous failures may temporarily create disconnected flooding topology regions, which is handled by temporarily adding links back to the flooding topology until the topology stabilizes.
sections.eli5: During normal times, updates flow along the chosen paths. If a chosen path breaks, routers use other paths temporarily until the leader figures out new routes.

sections.title: Deployment and Future Considerations
sections.content:
Dynamic Flooding supports gradual deployment. Routers supporting dynamic flooding can coexist with legacy routers. Flooding initiated on a dynamic-flooding router stays within the flooding topology until it reaches a legacy node, where standard flooding resumes. For correct operation, networks should deploy dynamic flooding on a connected set of routers in the dense areas, with legacy routers providing connectivity between separate dynamic-flooding regions only if necessary.

The exact optimal trade-offs between flooding topology density, convergence time, graph diameter, and node degree are topics for further study. Different applications may favor different flooding topologies based on their specific requirements.

RFC 9667 addresses IS-IS, OSPFv2, and OSPFv3. Security considerations focus on standard routing protocol protections; no new security mechanisms are introduced. IANA registrations include new TLV types and registry entries for standardized and private distributed algorithms, allowing future extensions without further standardization.
sections.eli5: This is experimental and may improve as operators test it. Old routers can still work alongside new ones. The gains are biggest in the dense areas where the problem is worst.

items.title: Redundant updates
items.text: Each update reaches a node multiple times through different paths.

items.title: Control plane overload
items.text: Processing redundant copies consumes CPU and bandwidth.

items.title: Delayed convergence
items.text: Update queues fill, causing legitimate updates to be dropped.

left.title: Standard flooding
left.desc: Updates flood along all available paths, causing redundancy.

right.title: Dynamic flooding
right.desc: Updates flow only along a computed topology that connects all nodes.
